en: The *Advayasiddhi*, composed by the Yoginī Lakṣmīṅkarā.
Oṃ! Homage to Śrī Vajrasattva!
Having bowed my head to the Lord, the omniscient one who arises from the three realms of existence, the naturally luminous Vajra who bestows the fruit of desired aims;
Without regard for place, time, lunar day, weekday, or constellations, nor even mandalas,
I shall now briefly describe the supreme sādhana of Vajrasattva.
One who practices yoga without the reality— through observances, vows, fasts, and meditations on the utterance of syllables— will not achieve perfection even in hundreds of millions of eons.

The practitioner of mantra should constantly worship himself with the internal emissions of the nose— feces, vajra-water, seed-syllables, and so forth— through the meditations on the principles of reality.
The knower of yoga should always worship his mother, sisters, daughters, and nieces by means of the application of wisdom and skillful means.
One should always honor women— even those who are deficient in a limb, low-born, artisans, or outcaste— by means of the cultivation of the splendor of the vajra of knowledge.
In this regard, these are the seed-syllables: Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ.
For by whatever means beings are bound through violent karma, by that very same means, when applied with skillful method, they are liberated from the bonds of existence.
One should perform the daily rites of the pledges (samaya) pertaining to the five families of the divine [deities],
and one should worship them with lamps and other offerings, including milk and substances originating from the universe.
With eyes wide open and a face always smiling, the minister,
having resolved his mind upon perfect enlightenment, should meditate on the ocean of gnosis.
Whatever stable or moving phenomena exist here within this abode of the three realms,
they should all be viewed through the yoga of reality as Vajradhṛk.
Furthermore, there are some proponents of other doctrines who are established through various distinctions of gender;
they too should not be disregarded here, for they are the miraculous manifestations of Vajrasattva.
Having made all phenomena equal through their emergence from selflessness,
the mantra-practitioner should constantly meditate upon the body as naturally stainless.

The All-pervading Lord is worshipped with perfumes, garlands, and the like, with garments, incense, and food offerings, as well as with songs, instrumental music, and dances, accompanied by skillful means.
One should not perform painful mental constructions, nor fasting, nor ritual action;
here there is neither bathing, nor purification, nor even the avoidance of village customs.
Nor should one worship gods made of wood, stone, or clay;
rather, being always composed, one should perform worship directed toward this very body.
One should worship the Holder of the Vajra with substances such as feces and urine, mixed with flies and vomit, and consecrated [with mantras], together with the five lamps.

The woman should worship the deity residing within her own body with self-originated flowers accompanied by milk— flowers that arise from the universe— through the contemplation of the fundamental principles (*tattva*).
One should steal the property of others, consort with the wives of others,
speak false words, and slay all the Buddhas.

One should not construct caityas made of stone, clay, or other materials; one should find no delight in books, nor should one perform mandalas even in a dream by means of the actions of body, speech, or mind.
The knower of mantras should never feel disgust toward any objects;
for Vajrasattva himself is present there in manifest form.

A practitioner of mantra who is fully concentrated should not entertain the conceptual distinction between those who may be approached and those who may not, nor likewise between what is edible and what is inedible, or what is drinkable and what is undrinkable.
One who knows the secret reality should consume living beings born from Vairocana and produced from the limbs of all creatures, for the sake of attaining accomplishment.
Women born from any of the castes are not to be despised;
she herself is the Blessed Lady Prajñā, having assumed a form through conventional reality (saṃvṛti).
Neither the lunar day nor the constellation, nor fasting, is prescribed for one endowed with non-dual knowledge; for such a person, the accomplishment of the Sugata arises.
What is the use of saying more here? Whatever is perceived, all that should be viewed through the yoga of reality by one who knows reality.
The knower of yoga should always consume the great lamp, which is mixed with the lamps produced from elephants, horses, donkeys, cows, camels, and dogs.
The knower of yoga should not form an attachment even to a single thing;
the ocean of existence is to be traversed through the yoga of a mind characterized by equanimity.
Arising, abiding, and cessation are not associated with ordinary beings;
yet when these exist, there is cyclic existence, and nowhere else is there dissolution or emergence.
The Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, is prescribed for the day, while Prajñā is prescribed for the night;
by meditating in this way, the yogi shall swiftly attain accomplishment.
That which is of unmanifest form, yet resides within all sentient beings—the supreme reality—is obtained from the mouth of the Guru; of this there is no doubt.
Non-abiding nirvana is signless and without abode;
it pervades all sentient beings—this is perfect enlightenment, the supreme state.
Thinking thus, the wise yogi who practices constantly will surely attain perfection; there is no doubt that even a man of meager merit shall succeed.
There is nothing higher than the teacher in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
by his grace, various accomplishments are attained by the wise.
He should indeed be known as Vajrasattva, to whom all Buddhas pay homage;
he is the supreme teacher, a god who must be worshipped with diligent effort.
He, whose nature is suchness, for the sake of favoring the world,
relies upon form and abides conventionally upon the seat of yoga.
This death is a conceptual construction which does not exist among any entities;
it is slain by one's own conceptualization through the manifestations of ordinary beings.

The *Sādhanopāyikā* named *Advayasiddhi*, which has emerged from the illustrious Oḍḍiyāna, reached the great seat of yoga (*mahāyogapīṭha*), contains within its womb the reality of all yoga-tantras, issued forth from the lotus-face of the illustrious Lakṣmī, and arises through the sequence of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*)—is hereby completed.
